notes.meaning: Nehemiah's enemies learned that the wall was completely rebuilt and had no gaps left. The only task remaining was hanging the heavy wooden doors in the gateways. Seeing the city almost secure, the enemies knew this was their last chance to stop the work.

Sanballat and Geshem sent a message asking Nehemiah to meet them in a village on the plain of Ono. This looked like a friendly offer to talk and settle their differences. Nehemiah saw through their trick, knowing they planned to kidnap or murder him away from the city.

Nehemiah sent messengers with a firm refusal, saying he was busy doing a great work and could not leave it. He wisely avoided mentioning that he knew about their plot. He simply explained that the building project was too important to be put on hold for a chat.

The enemies sent the exact same request four times in a row, hoping to wear Nehemiah down. Each time, Nehemiah gave the exact same answer. He refused to let repeated pressure pull him away from his duty.

Sanballat sent his servant a fifth time, but this time the servant carried an unsealed letter. Official letters to rulers were usually rolled up, tied, and sealed for privacy and respect. Leaving this letter open was a deliberate insult, and it allowed the public to read the scary rumors written inside.

The open letter claimed that the surrounding nations were buzzing with news that the Jews planned to rebel against the Persian king. It claimed that Geshem confirmed the story, and that Nehemiah was rebuilding the wall only to crown himself king.

The letter went on to accuse Nehemiah of hiring prophets in Jerusalem to declare him king over Judah. Sanballat warned that the Persian emperor would soon hear these rumors. He urged Nehemiah to meet with him right away to talk about how to handle the report.
Nehemiah sent back a direct and fearless reply. He stated that not a single thing in the letter was true. He told Sanballat plainly that he was inventing the entire story out of his own imagination.

Nehemiah saw that the enemies were only trying to terrify the Jews so their hands would drop from the work. Instead of panicking, he lifted his heart in a short prayer. He asked God to give strength to his hands so the work could be completed.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic translations follow the ancient Greek and Latin texts, understanding the end of the verse not as a prayer to God, but as Nehemiah's own resolve to redouble his efforts.

notes.meaning: Nehemiah visited Shemaiah, a man claiming to have a message from God who had shut himself up inside his house. Shemaiah warned that assassins were coming to murder Nehemiah that very night. He urged Nehemiah to run with him into the temple sanctuary and lock the doors for safety.

Nehemiah flatly refused to hide. As governor and leader, running away would show cowardice and discourage the entire community. Furthermore, God's law strictly forbade anyone who was not a priest from entering the inner sanctuary.

Nehemiah realized that God had never sent Shemaiah at all. A true prophet would never urge someone to break God's written law. Tobiah and Sanballat had paid Shemaiah money to deliver this false warning.

The enemies bribed the false prophet to make Nehemiah afraid enough to sin by entering the forbidden part of the temple. If Nehemiah had done that, they could have ruined his good name and destroyed his moral authority with the people.

Nehemiah prayed for God to remember what Tobiah, Sanballat, the false prophetess Noadiah, and the other corrupt prophets had done. Rather than seeking personal revenge, he placed the matter into the hands of the righteous Judge.

The wall was finished in only fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, which falls around September. This remarkable speed was possible because thousands worked with great devotion, repairing existing foundations and reusing stones already on the ground.

When the neighboring enemies heard the wall was finished, their pride fell and they lost their confidence. Even these hostile nations had to admit that the work could not have been done so quickly without God's help.

Even while the work went forward, several wealthy nobles of Judah carried on a steady exchange of letters with Tobiah. These leading men inside Jerusalem were keeping up friendly ties with a dangerous enemy of their own people.

Many in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah because of marriage alliances. Tobiah had married a Jewish woman from an important family, and his son had done the same. These family connections caused many Jewish leaders to take Tobiah's side over Nehemiah's.

These nobles kept praising Tobiah's good deeds to Nehemiah, while secretly reporting Nehemiah's words back to Tobiah. Meanwhile, Tobiah continued sending threatening letters to frighten Nehemiah into abandoning his work.
